2.label: Top: an undefended bishop developed to g4/g5 in the opening is grabbed for free by the queen (Qxg4/Qxg5); medium keeps the 'opening piece left en prise' theme but broadens to other hung pieces/pawns won by multi-move tactics (Bxf7+/Ng5+, Qb5+/Qa5+ forks, Nxc6, pawn grabs) plus some loosely-related king-weakening pawn moves.

12.label: Top: a quiet king/pawn move ignores doubled rooks on an open file, letting White win a rook/exchange with a forced Rxc8/Rxd8/Rxe8 capture sequence; medium keeps the 'quiet move that ignores a forcing tactic and hangs material' core but blurs the motif to any tactic (skewer, queen/diagonal check, deflection, back-rank mate, hanging minor).

11.label: Top: the defender abandons the critical stop/blockade duty and the opponent's passed pawn queens immediately (usually one move from promotion, often a 7th-rank/6th-rank pawn), frequently while greedily grabbing another pawn; medium keeps the same blockade-failure but blurs to slower cases where the passer merely advances with tempo or promotes over 2-3 moves, and the abandoned blockader varies across king, rook, and bishop (with a couple of near-equal tempo-loss outliers).

1.label: Top: a king move in pure king-and-pawn endgames that botches the decisive technique — losing the opposition, abandoning a key defensive pawn, or stepping off the promotion square — and throws away a win or draw; medium blurs to broader endings (passed-pawn, minor-piece and rook endgames, plus king-into-mating-net cases) where the king/piece placement is imprecise, and includes several borderline 0cp 'non-blunder' critical-king-move moments.

8.label: Top boards play a slow king/pawn/queen move instead of the thematic central pawn break (d4/d5/e5/f5), squandering a winning initiative on tempo; medium broadens to any passive, non-urgent move that fails the position's concrete demand — conceding a fork, a mating attack on the king, a passer, or lost counterplay.

6.label: Top: an early knight sortie (Ng5/Nb5/Nb4) hangs the knight outright and is refuted by a queen capture or check (Qxg5, Qa5+, Qa4+); medium keeps the premature-knight-thrust theme but the loss becomes subtler (removing a defender, getting trapped/traded) and occasionally extends to non-knight tempo-losing moves.

9.label: Top boards are uniformly greedy captures that open a file/diagonal and hang the queen for a minor piece; medium boards blur to careless moves dropping pawns or a piece, or walking the king into a forced mate.

3.label: At the peak the move hands the opponent a tempo-gaining/forcing reply in a critical one-good-move position (queen or rook chased, initiative lost); at medium this blurs into the king walking into a forced mating net (king-safety collapse) — and the broader set mixes tempo-loss, king-safety, and structural errors, so the unifying thread is only 'played the inferior move that lets the opponent's forcing line decide an already-precarious position.'

15.label: Top: a rook fails to control the enemy promotion square—often by greedily grabbing a pawn/piece elsewhere—letting the passer queen in a rook endgame; medium broadens the same promotion-race failure to king moves and wrong-target captures that also concede promotion (sometimes with check/skewer).

16.label: Top boards hang the queen with a forcing check that throws away a forced mate; medium boards still drop the queen for nothing but the check/forced-mate motif blurs into ordinary queen-en-prise blunders (sometimes via a piece vacating a defensive role).

7.label: At the peak the move is a king walk/castle straight into a winning attack or mate (Kc4# on the d-file, Kg3 into g4!, O-O-O into Nb5–Nd6+ fork); at medium it blurs to broader king-safety weakening and tempo-losing pawn/king moves (h7h6, Kb4) that concede the initiative rather than immediate material.

10.label: Top: in a winning endgame the player makes a natural king/knight move and clearly misses a decisive capture or passed-pawn push (often dxc3-style winning a piece, or pushing the queenside passer); medium broadens to subtler king-routing and tempo/move-order imprecisions (and a few near-best/false-positive moves).

4.label: Top fires on a piece moving to an exposed/undefended square that hangs material to a tactic in an already-worse position (with some false positives and one thrown win); medium broadens almost entirely into king-safety lapses—passive or wrong-side moves that ignore the one defensive resource and allow a decisive material-winning or mating attack.

14.chip: Hangs piece in opening (pawn at medium)
14.label: Top: a natural opening developing move (or unsound Bxf7+) ignores a pin/pawn-break threat (Bb5/Bg5/Bg4 + d5/e5/e4) and drops a full piece; medium blurs to the same 'ignore the threat in an opening position' lapse but losing only a pawn — or removing a key defender / once even missing a win.

0.label: Top: a center-closing pawn push or slow piece move that declines the decisive central capture/break (dxe4, exf6, dxc6, hxg6 e.p.), throwing away a winning/clearly-better center; medium keeps the 'slow move squanders the advantage' core but blurs into releasing pins (Bd2/Bh4 not Bxf6), skipping en-passant breaks (exd3, dxc3) and missing tactical shots (Bxh7), occasionally even hanging material (d6→Bxc6+).

17.chip: Hangs piece abandoning its duty (defender→exposed K/Q)
17.label: Top: in a won position a key defending/attacking piece is pulled off its duty (rook off the hanging-bishop capture, knight off passed-pawn support, bishop off the pawn it guards), hanging material; medium blurs into misplacing the king or queen onto a square that a rook hits with tempo (Rb7+/Rb5), squandering the win rather than dropping a piece outright.

13.label: At the peak, a move in a winning/better middlegame throws away the edge by overlooking a resource — missing the winning c3 fork (Bd2), allowing simplification, or permitting Qc8+ to win b7; at medium it narrows to the a6 case where ignoring White's threat lets g4 trap the bishop and win material, but the direction is genuinely mixed between hung material and missed wins.

19.label: Top boards hang a rook directly onto a square next to the enemy king in a won/drawn endgame (rook simply taken by the king, collapsing a win/mate into a draw); medium blurs the captured piece (queen/pawn as well as rook) and the capture mechanism, adding king-move-induced knight forks that win the queen.

21.label: Top: a quiet developing queen/bishop move in a balanced opening leaves a piece or pawn en prise to immediate capture (often the enemy queen) or allows mate after ignoring a standing threat; medium: the loss broadens to multi-move refutations—discovered attack, unsound sacrifice, or move-order error—still dropping material from an equal opening.

20.chip: Hangs material to ignored tactic (top fork)
20.label: Top: a passive/natural move ignores a forcing tactic—usually a knight fork or a tempo-check/king-hunt that wins material in a single demanding line; medium broadens to simply hanging a piece outright, a move-order slip, or a skipped defensive capture in already-difficult positions.

26.label: Top: the queen is moved to a square where it's immediately captured (often with check) delivering forced checkmate to a cornered king (king_safety); medium broadens to hanging any piece (rook/bishop/knight) for plain material, and even king-weakening or positional moves, so the constant 'queen-hung → mate' blurs to 'any-piece-hung → material loss'.

23.label: Top boards reposition the queen and decline the one defusing queen trade (Qxd3/Qxf3/Qxc6), exposing the king or dropping a pawn; medium boards broaden to any move that skips the saving queen trade, frequently leaving the queen or a rook outright hanging.

28.label: Top: in a winning rook endgame, directly hangs the rook en prise (often to the enemy king) while playing an unrelated pawn/piece move; medium blurs to throwing away the won ending more broadly — losing the rook to a skewer, or squandering the win via tempo-losing passive king/piece moves in pawn races.

31.label: Top: in a lost position the player declines a forced queen trade—typically via a pointless king move (or passive queen retreat)—leaving its own queen hanging or walking into mate; medium keeps the 'hangs your piece by ignoring the capture/trade' core but blurs the target to other pieces (rook, fork miscapture) beyond just the queen.

24.label: At the peak, an unforced king/pawn move exposes the player's own king to a decisive mating attack (king_safety collapse, often converting winning or losing into forced mate); at medium it blurs to quieter positional/endgame moves (Rd6, Ne4) that misplace a piece and hand back a won/equal position to opponent counterplay without an outright king hunt.

18.chip: Hangs piece on quiet move (often queen)
18.label: Peak: a calm/natural move (king or queen relocation, an 'attack' expecting a retreat) hangs the QUEEN in a winning position via a one-move capture or short forcing line; medium blurs into hanging lesser material (rook/bishop/exchange, short tactics) AND into materially-safe quiet moves that skip a winning capture or forcing shot.

30.label: At peak activation the player retreats/relocates a dominant attacking piece (usually a well-placed knight off f4/g5/g3/f6) and throws away a winning attack or initiative; at medium activation this blurs into any passive/quiet/natural move that skips the stronger forcing continuation and lets a winning or advantageous position slip to equality.

22.label: Top boards uniformly retreat/relocate the attacked f6-knight (Ng8/Ne4/Ng4/Nh5/Nd5) instead of the saving ...d5 break, losing tempo or hanging the knight; medium broadens to any piece (bishop, pawn, rook) played to escape or grab material while ignoring the board's decisive demand — hanging material, allowing mate, or missing a forced win.

29.label: Top is rock-solid: in a 100%-winning endgame the player drifts with a slow king-centralization or pawn-push instead of the clean rook-for-knight exchange sacrifice (Rxf6/Rxf5/Rxc6/Rxd6/Rxe4/Rxf3, once a bishop on e6) that liquidates the opponent's lone minor piece into a trivially won pawn ending; medium blurs the piece and the precision, becoming a general 'skipped the precise forcing conversion in a better position' that also bleeds into outright hanging material (back-rank Re5, Kc6 skewer, Rxh7 zwischenzug) as the enemy knight/bishop springs back to life.

34.chip: Exposed own king to attack (knight/king move)
34.label: TOP boards are king-safety blunders that expose one's own king to a winning attack (a defending piece vacating, the king wandering, or a pawn weakening), plus one outlier missing a back-rank mate; MEDIUM narrows to a knight reroute and a king march that walk into forking checks and lose material.

33.label: Top boards relocate a piece (or the king itself) off critical kingside defense, exposing the king to a decisive/mating attack (Nb3, Rfa1, Kf5, Kd1); medium blurs to abandoning any key defender so that a pawn or piece (h4, d4, b5, the bishop) simply hangs, sometimes via tempo-loss or a careless pawn push.

36.label: Top boards are queen moves that vacate a key defensive square and let a forced mating attack crash into the own king; medium broadens to pawn pushes, king walks, and castling-into-it that loosen the king's cover (and sometimes just drop material rather than force mate).

35.label: Top: from a lost position the player declines the only saving queen trade (Qxg5/Qxe4/Qxf6 etc.) and a queen/king/pawn move walks into a FORCED CHECKMATE; medium: the same king-exposing/passive move instead just allows checks that win material (e.g. a rook via Qb5+ or a pin) rather than immediate mate.

38.label: Top boards center on a queen moved to a vulnerable square that loses material—either placed directly en prise (Qf5 grabbed by the bishop) or driven around / lost to a tempo-gaining hit (Qe6, Qf5, Qxd2→Qc8+); medium blurs to any major-piece misplacement, adding rook excursions (Rd6, Rd7, Rg8) and defender-removing bishop retreats (Bc8) that drop material to a tempo-gaining refutation.

32.label: Top boards are materially-safe quiet/positional moves that expose the king or remove a defender and walk into a decisive check/mate over a few ply (Bc5→Rg4+...mate, Rd7→Qa3+, dxe7→Bxc3+); medium narrows to pure positional concessions—trading off the dominant piece (Nxe7) or removing a key pawn's support (b3→Qd3)—that surrender a winning/equal position without any single-ply material loss.

41.label: Top: a queen capture-with-check trades into a 'won' simplification but throws away a forced mate; medium blurs to rook/bishop captures and wrong-order captures that squander a clearly winning position into a draw (or a loss when the capture frees an enemy promotion).

25.label: Top: a greedy capture (almost always rook-takes-bishop) that strips the sole back-rank defender and loses to forced back-rank mate — or lets an enemy passed pawn promote; medium blurs away from captures to king walks (Kf1/Kb3/Kg8), pawn pushes, and piece misplacements that overlook other decisive tactics (forks, Greek-gift/king attacks, promotions).

45.label: Top: a rook move abandons the back-rank defender so Black mates immediately (Qxc1#); medium: a rook move removes a key defender/blocker (deflection, discovered-attack screen), enabling a king-side tactic that wins material rather than mating.

44.label: Top boards play a prophylactic/repositioning move (king-step, pawn push, queen shuffle) that abandons defense and hangs a major piece—most sharply the a8-rook on a long queen diagonal; medium blurs this to any non-forcing move that drops material more generally (pawn, exchange, or back-rank collapse as in Qd2 blocking the d-file).

46.label: In completely winning endgames the player makes a materially-safe move (often a greedy capture) that fails to take the cleanest path; at the peak it's skipping a concrete forced mate (mate-in-1 or a thrown-away forced mate), while at medium it blurs into mere tempo/efficiency loss — delaying the win or grabbing an irrelevant pawn in an already-won endgame, frequently with 0cp loss.

27.label: Top: in a won/equal endgame a quiet king move forfeits material by skipping a decisive free queen/rook capture and usually hangs its own piece in the refutation; medium narrows to a king move that merely lets a free rook escape — a materially-safe missed win.

42.label: Top: a quiet opening move (Be6/h6/e6) lets a White knight capture the g6/e6 bishop, forcing ...fxg6/fxe6 into shattered doubled pawns and an exposed king on the open f-file (material even but positionally lost); medium blurs to other opening moves that allow knight forks (Nb5–c7, Nc2+) or tempo-losing knight blows that win material outright.

53.label: Top boards squander a forced mate/win into a dead draw in queen-vs-pawn/king-pawn endgames; medium boards blur into mere tempo losses (or even engine-optimal moves) within already-won endgames.

51.label: Top boards uniformly promote a winning passed pawn straight into an enemy bishop/knight capture, hanging the brand-new queen; medium boards broaden to prematurely pushing or greedily abandoning a dominant passed pawn for short-term material, losing its strategic value.

43.label: Top boards are quiet king-centralization moves in already-lost endgames that choose an inferior/passive defensive route (Kc6, Kf6, Ke6), failing the most resilient defense and hastening the collapse; medium blurs the constant 'king move' into other materially-safe passive moves in lost endgames — luft/space pawn pushes (h4) and rook shuffles (Rd8) — that likewise speed the loss, with magnitudes ranging from a few cp to forced mate (and a few boards where the played move is actually best), making the signal genuinely mixed.

37.label: Top: clearly-winning positions (100% winning) thrown away by a move that hangs own material—peak cases are greedy rook grabs (Rxh7) and king-exposing pawn/king moves; medium blurs into merely-better or near-equal positions undone by an assorted mix of king-safety blunders, tempo losses, and hung pieces, so the unifying 'hangs material to a decisive refutation' thread holds but the specific motif varies widely.

49.label: Top: a passive/defensive non-capturing move (king tuck, pawn push, piece retreat) in a losing position permits a forced mate or king-safety collapse; medium blurs to the same passivity allowing general winning tactics (forks, pins, dark-square ruin, won pawns) or skipping a clean win.

52.label: At the peak it's a clearly-winning side declining a direct hanging-piece capture (67.Kxa3 over Kc2, 34...Rxc4 over Rd8); at medium it blurs into slow king/tempo moves (Kf8, Ke7, Bf6) that skip the only winning continuation and let a won position slip to a draw.

48.label: Top: a forcing check (usually a saving perpetual or intermezzo) was the only/best resource but the player instead grabbed material or made a slow move, throwing away the draw/win; medium: broadens to any non-forcing, tempo-losing move (passive piece shuffle, quiet pawn push, wrong move-order) that surrenders the initiative when a check was the strongest continuation.

57.label: Top: a knight jumps in with check intending a fork/discovery from a winning position but is simply captured (hxg/Rx/Qx) for nothing; medium keeps the knight-check-that-hangs core but blurs to capture-checks (Nxf6+/Nxc6+), occasional queen checks, and move-order/missed-mate variants.

60.label: Top boards are clean forced mates (mate in 2-6) thrown away by a slow/distracting move that surrenders the decisive tempo or abandons the key mating piece; medium blurs to squandering a winning advantage more broadly — imprecise checks, captures or piece shuffles that miss the one precise continuation (sometimes a positional/material edge rather than mate).

56.label: Top: in an already-lost position the king/queen drifts off defense, skipping the one defensive capture/trade of an attacking (often second) queen and converting a survivable loss into forced mate; medium broadens to passive pawn pushes (back-rank, king-shield removal) that simply allow the immediate mating net.

54.label: Top: a passive pawn move in a clearly winning position throws away the win (e.g. h3 ignoring Qxa7); medium broadens to king/queen moves and merely-unclear positions where the quiet, non-forcing move instead allows a tactical refutation (pawn storm, back-rank mate, Rd2+/Bxa7 winning material).

50.label: At peak the player overlooks an available checkmate (almost always mate-in-one) by playing a natural attacking/developing move; at medium it blurs into missing a winning tactic or simply hanging material with a tempting but flawed active move that throws away a won position.

55.label: At the peak it's a pawn capture/push (often recapturing on d5) that opens a line—usually the a2-g8 diagonal for an enemy bishop (Bxd5) or the g-file before the king—hanging material to a tactic; medium activations blur to any greedy capture or defender-abandoning move that drops material to the refutation.

61.label: Top boards are uniformly a knight fork delivered WITH CHECK that wins a rook/queen in a won endgame (player instead made a passive king move or wrong check); medium keeps the 'missed a forcing winning check' core but blurs the tactic/piece — rook forks, bishop forks, discovered attacks, skewers and double-attack checks.

63.label: Top boards are premature opening queen sorties that directly hang a piece — the queen itself or the piece/pawn it stopped defending; medium broadens to the over-extended queen (occasionally a rook) being chased with tempo and only then dropping material or position.

47.label: Top: the queen wanders to the a-file/rim (Qa5, Qa1, Qa8, Qa4, Qxa2, Qa6) and deserts kingside defense, so a forcing check/mate or perpetual sequence crashes through; medium keeps the offside/flank-queen idea (Qa4, Qxa7, Qe6, Qc4) but blurs into other pieces and pawn pushes (Kg1, Re5, Rd3, d3, Nf5) that likewise neglect king safety, sometimes only bleeding material or tempo rather than the king.

64.label: At the peak, an already-winning side skips a forcing capture of the enemy queen (usually WITH CHECK, e.g. Qxh5+/Qxf2+/Qxd7+) and so throws away a forced mate; at medium it broadens to any missed mate-keeping forcing move (tempo loss in the attack, declined sacrifice, greedy pawn-grab over Qxe5+), with several flagged boards actually being 0cp non-blunders that dilute the signal.

66.chip: Hangs major piece, won endgame (often via check)
66.label: Top: a trivially winning endgame is thrown away by hanging a major piece (queen or rook), most often with a check the enemy king just captures; medium shows the same rook-hung-via-check motif (Rf8+→Kxf8), with milder tempo/promotion cases as noisy tails.

58.label: At the peak a developed minor piece is hung outright to a direct tactic (Bg5 lost to ...Bxg5/Qxg5, or Nf7 taken free); at medium it broadens to knights pushed to attackable outposts (Nf5 hit by g4) and rook misplacements (Rf3) that don't drop material cleanly but invite a king attack or squander a winning position.

65.label: Top boards hang material outright in an equal opening via opened lines or en-prise pieces (rook on d4d5, pawn on Bc5, queen on Qxg2); medium boards broaden to king-weakening pawn/rook moves (g6, Rc8) that lose material a few moves later through checks and piece invasions.

62.label: Top boards are king moves (Kf3, Kf3, Ke8) that walk into forcing check/mate sequences—pure king-safety failures in near-balanced endgames; medium blurs to quiet non-king moves (Be2, a4, h6) that ignore a central tactical threat (undefended d4, the ...e4 fork, dark-square weakening), with each conceding material to the opponent's forcing refutation rather than meeting the threat.

59.label: Top boards consistently misplace a strongly-placed piece — retreating an active attacker (Bh3) or rook from the assault, or walking the king into danger — abandoning the forcing/winning continuation; medium blurs this into premature queen sorties and repositionings that surrender tempo and squander the winning advantage, but the direction is genuinely mixed (some pure missed-wins, some multi-move material loss/mate).

73.label: Top: in drawn/winning endgames the king marches to an exposed square (Kd8/Kg5/Kf5/Ke5) that is punished by forced mate via checks; medium blurs to the same king-walk but where the refutation just wins material via checks/forks rather than mating (and one outlier is a knight wandering into a trap).

70.label: Top: an undefended enemy queen sitting free to be captured is ignored; medium: same missed free capture but the hanging target broadens to any piece (rook, bishop, or knight).

68.label: At the peak the player drops a piece to a simple, often one-move capture—frequently by moving its own defender or capturing without support; at medium activation it broadens to losing material via varied tactical motifs (pins, forks, discovered attacks, trapped pieces, king-safety collapses) plus some outright missed winning captures.

72.label: Top: a speculative queen sortie (usually Qh3-type) abandons a key defensive duty and hangs material or allows mate; medium broadens to any piece (and pawn) that quits a defensive/restraining job or walks into a threat, with a sizable minority being missed forcing captures rather than hangs.

71.label: Top: a premature QUEEN check against an uncastled e1-king (Qa5+/Qa4+/Qh4+) that the opponent simply blocks with an interposition gaining tempo, squandering the player's edge; medium broadens to BISHOP development checks (Bb4+/Bb5+) and Qh5+ that likewise waste tempo, with outcome split ~50/50 between pure tempo loss and dropping material in the refutation after the block.

67.label: Top: in Spanish/Italian-style openings White hangs the light-squared bishop on a4/b5 to the ...b5 pawn break (or skips the Bxc6+ capture that resolves the c-file tension); medium blurs to any opening minor piece left hanging or harassed by a pawn push (hxg4, g5, axb4), mixed with a few missed Bxc3+/fork shots.

69.label: Top: in an already-winning position, plays a natural/greedy move that fails to capture the hanging or forkable enemy queen; medium broadens to other squandered decisive wins — forced mate, pawn promotion, or hanging one's own piece while skipping the kill.

74.label: Top: in an already-lost endgame the player makes a move (king tuck or greedy pawn-grab) that walks straight into a clean forced mate, usually back-rank or open-file; medium broadens to moves that allow a slower forced mate or merely decisive material loss (promotion with tempo, exchange via skewer, queen-for-rook), so the constant 'mate-in-a-lost-position' blurs into general material collapse.

77.label: Top boards hang a piece outright to a one-move recapture (queen/rook/knight after a careless capture or check, or ignoring a standing threat); medium boards broaden to material dropped via deeper tactics (forks, pins, opened lines) and bleed into missed forced mates and mere inaccuracies.

84.label: Top boards almost always hang the queen — typically a routine developing/king move while a bishop or knight directly attacks Qd8 (refuted by Bxd8/Nxg8), missing the obvious recapture; medium blurs to hanging any piece (bishops to a pawn on e5, queen to Nf6) and shades into failing to grab a loose enemy piece, so own-material loss is constant but the piece and pure-hang-vs-missed-capture distinction varies.

83.label: Top is uniformly a missed knight leap to b5/b4 threatening Nc7+/Nxc2+ to fork king and rook in a winning opening; medium broadens to other missed winning knight jumps/tactics (Nd5, Nxe4, Nxd5) and occasionally drifts into allowed-fork or even hung-piece (Nh6) cases.

78.label: At the peak, a quiet king/pawn move (Kd7, g5, Ne5) exposes the king to a forced mating attack while ahead; at medium it blurs to any tempo-losing or repositioning quiet move (Ke1/Kf2 walks, Qd7 retreats, Nh2 reroute) that squanders a winning or equal position to the opponent's tactical refutation.

81.label: Top: a clearly winning position (often a passed-pawn endgame) is spoiled by a materially-safe but slow or greedy move that skips the unique decisive continuation such as pushing the passer; medium broadens to passive tempo-losing piece moves—queen retreats, king shuffles—that throw away the win without ever losing material.

85.label: Top boards hang the player's own piece by moving into a capture/pin or abandoning a defender amid piece tension; medium boards keep that loose-piece theme but blur to also include failing to capture a hanging enemy piece (missed forced wins) and slow moves that surrender a winning advantage.

86.label: Top: a quiet developing/retreating move overlooks a knight capture of a hanging central pawn (Nxd5/Nxe4/Nxd4) when best-move wins material; medium blurs to other missed pawn-winning tactics, breaks and squandered edges, all in materially-safe non-capturing positions.

76.label: Top: a knight (also a queen/bishop) deserts a critical central defensive post (d5/d3 outpost, f7-guard) and is punished by invasion, promotion, or being trapped offside; medium blurs to aggressive pawn pushes (f5) and developing moves (Nc3) that likewise skip the needed tactical defense and drop material.

75.label: Top: a clearly won position is blown by one imprecise move (peak: a safe rook move missing the winning capture 33...cxd2); medium blurs to equal/winning endgame conversions where the lone precise move is skipped (pawn-push move-order, king-walk-into-mate), flipping the game into a loss — mistake direction split between missed wins and hung material.

87.label: Top boards are opening moves—mostly premature pawn pushes (a5, e5, c4) plus queenside castling—that squander a clear edge and lose material to a forcing refutation; the lone medium board narrows to a knight retreated onto an attacked square (Nd7), a direct hang.

89.label: At the peak, the player is in a won position with a forced mate and plays a less-forcing move that misses immediate checkmate or extends the mate distance (often skipping a tempo-gaining check); at medium activation this blurs into general tempo-losing/inefficient conversion in already-winning endgames, including several near-0cp non-blunders and a few cases where the slower move actually concedes material in the refutation.

82.label: Top boards squander a won position by allowing a saving perpetual check—usually after a greedy queen/rook capture or a king-safety lapse; medium broadens to king-walks and pawn-shield breaks that concede either perpetual check or an outright (often back-rank) mate.

88.chip: Hangs king to attack (mate at peak)
88.label: Top boards are king-safety moves that walk straight into forced checkmate (Kc1→mate, g6 blocks the escape square→mate), while medium blurs to milder king-exposing/kingside-weakening moves (Kf7 into a rook check, h6) that merely surrender king safety or initiative without immediate mate.

79.label: Top: while winning, captured the enemy queen into an unfavorable trade—often in the wrong capture order, so the recapture wins the player's own queen back (or more)—squandering the win; medium: the same wrong-order queen capture (Bxd8 hangs the c3 queen), while weaker activations blur toward greedy pawn-grabs and tempo-losing checks.

91.chip: Traded into lost pawn endgame (key defender)
91.label: Top boards uniformly capture/trade the dark-squared bishop into a clearly lost (or won→drawn) king-and-pawn endgame; medium keeps the 'eliminated the only defensive piece' theme but blurs to knight trades and other endgame types — minor-piece endgames, tempo-wasting captures, and promotion/passed-pawn races (plus a stray case where the capture was actually forced/best).

102.label: Top boards uniformly hang the queen to a bishop sweeping an open diagonal (g5/h4–d8 or g4–d1), usually by moving a pawn/piece that unblocked the line or failing to address the bishop's attack; medium keeps this queen-to-diagonal-bishop theme but broadens to also include hanging a rook (e.g. Bxh8) to the same long-diagonal bishop.

100.label: Top: unsound knight capture on f7 or f2 expecting a royal fork / Fried Liver but simply recaptured by the king, dropping a full piece for a pawn in the opening; medium broadens to other speculative kingside knight sacs (including Greek-gift Nxh7) refuted by rook/queen recapture or zwischenzug rather than only Kx.

90.label: Top boards are premature passed-pawn moves (pushes like e2/b2/d2 or grabs like cxb7/fxg7) that skip a preparatory check/piece move and get the pawn blockaded, captured, or walk into mate — squandering a winning edge; medium broadens to any premature pawn advance/capture (c3, e4, h4, axb4, exf7) plus a few hanging piece moves, blurring between hanging material and throwing away a forced win.
