191.label: Top boards are all purposeless rook checks in losing endgames—roughly half hang the rook outright (Ra8+, Rd1+), half just waste a tempo and drive the enemy king to a better/more central square; medium broadens to knight/queen/bishop checks and to giving a check instead of grabbing free material (Rxe6, bxc6, Qxb5).

196.label: TOP: pure king-and-pawn endgames where the king steps off the only opposition/front-of-pawn square, flipping a dead draw into forced mate; MEDIUM broadens to passed-pawn blockade and active-king/tempo king moves that merely squander the win or advantage.

192.chip: Hangs piece via undefending move (mate/exchange→lost edge)
192.label: Top: a move—often a capture—abandons a defender, hanging the rook/exchange or walking into a forced back-rank/king-hunt mate; medium: the same undefending/relocating idea but no clean hang, instead a bad trade or allowed fork that surrenders a winning advantage.

195.label: Top boards consistently play a quiet/safe move that throws away a forced king-side mate (usually Qg7#-type); medium keeps the king-attack context but blurs to missing any decisive resource — winning sacs/attacks, a saving perpetual, or a promotion threat — and a few tip into outright hangs/positional collapses.

190.chip: Hangs piece grabbing queen (or missed mate)
190.label: Top: recaptures the enemy QUEEN immediately and hangs own piece by skipping a saving zwischenzug check (usually Nxe7+); medium broadens to grabbing material on the obvious square instead of a forced mate or stronger forcing intermediate, shifting from hung-piece to missed-win.

194.label: Top boards capture/trade queens to 'simplify' away a winning or attacking position; medium blurs to other advantage-conceding moves, chiefly the positional ...g6 king-weakening push, so the unifying thread is voluntarily surrendering a won/safe position rather than queen trades specifically.

205.label: Top: in a winning position the player skips an undefended knight on g5/g4 that the queen could grab for free (Qxg5/Qxg4), playing a routine developing/prophylactic move instead; medium broadens to missing any free capture of an undefended piece or pawn by any piece (Bxe2, Nxe7, Nxe4, Qxd6), with a few noisier tempo/king-safety cases.

193.label: Top: a quiet king/pawn move vacates a guarded square (or the king's shield), inviting a forcing tempo reply—check, fork, skewer, or invasion—that wins material or mates; medium keeps the abandoned-square theme but broadens to greedy captures and other piece moves and occasionally just a missed win rather than a clean hang.

202.label: Top boards hang the queen by capturing (usually with check) into an immediate king recapture, collapsing a winning or mating endgame into a draw/much-reduced edge; medium broadens to rooks, pawn-promotions, and queen trades recaptured by king or pawn.

204.label: Top: pawn-endgame king moves that skip the one forced pawn capture/exchange (gxf5, fxg5, dxc4), letting the opponent build a winning passed pawn and flip a draw/win into a loss; medium blurs to other slow tempo-wasting moves (rook/bishop, non-pawn endgames) that similarly concede a passer or drop material.

201.label: Top boards squander a winning position by botching a confrontation with a strong enemy BISHOP (challenging, trading, or fleeing it) and dropping material to the refutation; medium blurs the target to other strong pieces (the queen) and the failure mode to tempo/king-safety collapse rather than a clean piece-hang.

189.label: Top boards are inferior/pointless queen checks (Qe5+, Qd5+) that let the king reach safety or allow a queen interposition, squandering a winning attack; medium blurs to general tempo-wasting moves in won positions (h6, a5) plus a check that throws away a forced mate (Qf2+), all materially-safe moves that fail to play the decisive continuation.

207.label: Top boards uniformly miss a one-move capture of the opponent's hanging/undefended QUEEN in an already-won position (often playing a flashy check instead); medium boards blur to overlooking free captures of any hanging piece (rook/bishop) and a few other 'only-move' wins (promotion/tempo/back-rank defense).

203.label: Top: a king move (or king-loosening move) in an already-winning middlegame walks straight into a forced mating attack — back-rank/corner queen mate or rook invasion against the exposed monarch; at medium the king-mate component blurs away into similar passive/weakening moves that merely leak tempo or a pawn (h3, h6, d8) as the opponent's heavy pieces activate, rather than delivering mate.

197.label: Top: king declines the only-move recapture Kxf7 (plays Kf8/Kf1/Kd2 or a quiet move) in opening sac/fork lines, hanging a piece or the queen; medium broadens to general king-misplacement blunders — moving the king into checks, mate, or back-rank trouble, mishandling king safety, and occasionally other declined recaptures (Kxg7).

213.label: Top boards consistently dump a full minor/major piece outright in the opening to a one-move free capture (Ba6, Nc3 into d4, Qg5, Nxd5); medium broadens to dropping a pawn, the exchange, or a piece via short tactical/positional refutations rather than instant one-move hangs.

199.label: Top boards are greedy pawn-grab captures (Qxb2, Qxg5, Nxe6, Rxf3) that hang material to a multi-move tactical refutation; medium broadens to non-capturing piece misplacements (c4, Bd1, Qa4) that abandon a defensive/blockading duty and lose material to the same kind of tactic.

208.label: Top: a passive move (usually a queen retreat like Qh2/Qg7/Qd8) skips an available forcing CHECK that would mate, win, or hold a perpetual; medium broadens to any passive/misplaced move that forfeits a winning edge, where the missed continuation is no longer strictly a check (luft like h4, rook activity Rc7/Rg-file, or a queen-trade).

206.label: Top boards are forced mates where the king walks in or a greedy capture opens lines onto it; medium boards keep the king-safety theme but blur to king moves/captures that merely drop material (knight forks, hanging pieces) or miss a winning shot rather than force mate.

211.label: Top boards almost all hang a rook outright via a king or rook move that abandons it; medium blurs into losing other material (bishop), wasting tempo, or making a king move that allows a mating attack.

215.label: Top: ...Bg4 pinning the Nf3 to the queen, uniformly refuted by Bxf7+ then a Ng5+/Ne5+ fork winning the g4-bishop; medium broadens to other bishop pins/developments (Bb4, Bb5) that hang material to assorted opening tactics like Qa4+ forks, e5 pushes, or Nxe4.

214.label: Top: in a winning opening, an undefended enemy piece (almost always the g4 bishop) is chased with f3 or blocked with Be2 instead of simply grabbed by Qxg4; medium keeps the 'one precise winning move ignored in a better position' idea but blurs from clean free captures into broader squandering — passive pawn/developing moves that miss other tactical shots or even allow counterplay (forks, Qh5, missed mate).

212.label: Top boards uniformly move the queen onto a knight-attacked square in the opening, hanging it for free; medium boards still hang a piece into a one-move capture but broaden to rooks (and an occasional minor) and to non-knight capturers (pawn, rook, king) in the middlegame.

216.label: Top boards are queen moves that offer/allow a queen exchange simplifying a winning-or-holdable position into a lost (usually pawn) endgame; medium keeps the simplification theme but blurs to rook trades and other advantage-squandering liquidations into draws.

218.label: Top: in a winning rook endgame a quiet king/pawn move skips the forcing rook check/skewer (or mate-in-1/3) that wins material or mates; medium keeps the 'winning endgame, played a non-forcing move' core but blurs the winning motif to knight forks, queen trades, and move-order tempo with other pieces.

209.chip: Hangs piece in won game (or missed win)
209.label: Top boards constantly squander a winning position by hanging a piece—frequently a greedy grab of a 'free' target that gets recaptured; medium boards blur the direction toward materially-safe moves that miss the win (throwing away forced mates/winning tactics or drifting), so the unifying theme is 'blew a won game' but the mechanism splits between hanging material (peak) and missing the win (medium).

217.label: Top boards all decline the single winning CAPTURE of a hanging enemy piece (often the passer's blockader) in a won endgame, pushing a pawn instead; medium keeps the 'skipped the only winning move in a won endgame' frame but blurs from capture to precise pawn move-order / king-tempo plays.

220.label: TOP: in a winning/drawn passed-pawn endgame, played a slow king/knight move instead of immediately pushing the passer, squandering the tempo race; MEDIUM broadens the slow-move piece to rooks and adds greedy captures/missed tactical shots (plus a few borderline non-blunders) that likewise waste the critical promotion tempo.

226.chip: Hangs piece to king recapture (often rook)
226.label: Top: a rook gives a check that the king simply captures, dumping a won position (often into a pawn endgame); medium broadens to queens, bishops and pawns plus lopsided trades (queen/bishop-for-rook) that liquidate the win into a drawn or lost ending.

210.label: Top: a 'simplifying' queen-trade offer (Qe2/Qd2-type) played instead of the sole saving king move, losing material or a lost pawn endgame to the refutation; medium blurs to any tempting rook/king/pawn move that hangs material or exposes the king to a forcing check sequence.

227.label: Top: a bishop developed to g4 or g5 hangs outright (Nxg4/Nxg5, or ...Bxf3 winning a pinned knight); medium broadens to other premature bishop sorties (Bf4, tempo-losing or newly-unpinned bishops) that still drop a piece or a key tempo.

224.label: Top: a repositioning move (king/rook/pawn/knight) in a winning endgame deserts the defense of an own pawn, conceding it for free; medium keeps the abandon-the-defender mechanism but broadens the lost unit to minor pieces and to smaller tempo-loss drops.

219.label: Top boards consistently fail to promote a passed pawn immediately — playing a king move or pointless check instead of an immediate (often promotion-with-check) queening that wins or forces mate; medium boards blur into broader winning-endgame imprecision, mixing pawn-race tempo losses with outright hung pieces.

221.label: Top boards are greedy bishop/knight captures that grab a pawn or minor piece while leaving the queen or a rook hanging to the refutation; medium broadens to any move — quiet piece relocations (Ne4, Bf4, Nc3) and pawn pushes — that simply leave a piece en prise or walk into a decisive material/king-safety loss.

225.label: At the peak a developing/advancing move surrenders a key central square — releasing tension to gift an enemy knight outpost (f5/d5) or abandoning its own e4; at medium it blurs into broader passive or wrong-square/wrong-geometry moves that waste a tempo and concede initiative, mixed with some outright king-safety blunders.

231.label: At the peak the move is a passive piece retreat (often a bishop, e.g. Bb3/Bf4) that abandons a clearly winning attack or edge while staying materially safe; at medium it blurs into any non-capturing, non-checking repositioning move (rook lift, queen/pawn shuffle) that throws away the won position and invites a tactical or positional refutation.

230.label: Top: a king-safety move (king walking into a net or removing/blocking its own defender) that allows a forced mate in an already-losing position; medium broadens to any self-destructive move that hangs a piece to a fork/check or otherwise worsens a lost position.

234.label: Top boards center on the king/rook move that mishandles the critical rook-trade pawn-endgame transition (allowing Rxc4+ or missing Rxf5/Rxe4+); medium broadens to any rook/king endgame move that squanders a winning or drawn result — d2+ tempo loss or Kc5 hanging the rook — mixing 'hangs material' with 'missed conversion'.

232.chip: Traded queen into lost ending (med: hangs)
232.label: Top: a queen-capture check trades into a lost K+P endgame, forfeiting the perpetual-check or pawn-stopping resource the queen provided; medium broadens to hanging the queen outright via a check the king just takes (KxQ), plus borderline non-blunder simplifications.

235.chip: Hangs piece to pawn break (often bishop)
235.label: Top: a bishop is placed/kept on a square where an enemy pawn thrust forks or traps it, losing material; medium broadens to queens and knights skewered by the same pawn breaks, with a few missed tactical shots and positional slips mixed in.

222.label: Top: a tempting active/recapturing move surrenders the player's own king safety (a defender or pawn shelter), punished by a kingside attack; medium broadens to abandoning any key square/file/duty (back rank, open file, blockade, counterplay), often losing material in the refutation and occasionally just missing a tactic.

239.label: Top: player grabs a rook sitting on a back-rank/promotion square (d1/e1/c1/b1/e8/h8), and the recapturing pawn promotes to a queen WITH CHECK, delivering immediate or forced back-rank mate; medium keeps the 'captured a piece that frees an enemy pawn to promote on the recapture' idea but blurs the punishment — the promotion often just wins material or queens a passed pawn rather than mating, with a few cases where the freed unit isn't a promotion at all.

236.label: Top boards consistently miss an elementary opening capture/recapture that wins a free piece (usually a bishop, often with a pawn); medium blurs to other squandered-opening errors — missed pawn-wins and non-capturing pushes (e.g. g5) that allow a tactical refutation.

238.label: Top: rook/pawn-endgame moves that skip a tempo-gaining intermediate check (Ra3+, Rd7+) or key push, losing the promotion race or walking into a back-rank mate; medium broadens to general tempo/move-order slips — missed checks, abandoned open files, greedy captures — that let the opponent promote or win material, with a couple of outright hangs (skewer, discovered attack, undefended rook).

229.chip: Wrong plan-move squanders advantage (often pawn push)
229.label: Top: a tempting 'improving' move — most often a pawn advance, sometimes a piece sortie — throws away a clearly winning or holding position where exactly one precise move was required (huge swings); medium: the same wrong-plan/tempo-loss pattern with smaller swings, blurring into one-square misses, missed wins, and greedy pawn-grabs.

242.label: Top boards are quiet positional moves — pawn pushes (g6, c4) and bishop misplacements (Be3) — that hand White a dominant central square/diagonal for its pieces (Nd6 outpost, Qd4 center, Bb1 diagonal) with a ~200–265cp swing; the medium case narrows to a single passive bishop retreat (Bd7) that loses tempo and cedes the center to White's queen, with one outlier (Bxg5) actually hanging the piece outright.

240.label: Top boards are already winning and consistently miss a piece-winning Bxf3-style bishop-takes-knight capture (or wrong-ordered version) that exploits an overloaded/pinned defender; medium blurs to any precise capture or recapture move-order in a favorable position (Bxd1, Bxb3, Qxc7, cxd5, Nxe4), with a few hanging own material rather than purely skipping the win.

245.chip: Hangs queen via e4-discovery (else king attack)
245.label: Top: moving the e4 knight off the open e-file hangs the queen to Nc6+ discovered check; medium broadens to greedy grabs (Nxf2, lose minor piece) and king-weakening pawn moves (...f6 → Qh5+ sac) that lose material the same way.

246.label: Top: ignores an en-prise enemy piece (usually an unrecaptured bishop on f3/f6) with a quiet developing/castling move and drops a full piece; medium broadens to loosening pawn pushes or piece sorties that ignore a tactical weakness, typically dropping just a pawn.

247.label: At the peak a developing/grabbing move (Bg5, Nxe5, h3, Nxe4) ignores the queens facing off on the open d-file and hangs the e4-pawn or e5-knight after the forced ...Qxd1+/Kxd1; at medium the same skip of the with-check Qxd1+/Qxd8+ trade blurs into losing castling rights, wasting tempo, or allowing a Nd5/Nxc7+ fork rather than dropping a clean piece.

244.label: Top boards are passive/irrelevant moves in already-lost positions that ignore the only defense and allow or accelerate forced mate (king safety); medium boards keep the same 'neglected the critical resource' flaw but the cost broadens to material—walking into forks, hanging pieces, greedy grabs that abandon the king, or missed tactical wins—rather than checkmate.

253.label: Top: pushing a passed pawn to the queening/penultimate square so White's king or rook blockades in front and captures the freshly-promoted queen; medium broadens to any premature passed-pawn advance that lets the king blockade and win it — but the medium set is noisy, mixing genuine push-into-blockade errors with several 0cp non-blunders and a stray fork.

250.label: Top: a winning side drops its queen onto a square where an enemy rook just grabs it (…Qe5 → Rxe5) in a won endgame; medium blurs to broader careless squandering of the won position — a tempo-losing queen detour or a rook move that lets the opponent escape with perpetual check.

251.label: Top: in completely won positions the player skips the decisive rook trade (Rxf2+, Rxc7+, Rxg8, etc.) that liquidates into a winning K+P endgame, playing a slow non-forcing move instead; medium broadens to any missed forcing/precise move — favorable queen trades, forcing capture sequences (Rxb8+, Bxg2+), Qxd7+ — plus a few outright material hangs.

256.label: Top: in a winning opening the player ignores the simple e5xf6 pawn capture that grabs a hanging knight, instead playing a developing/center move; medium broadens to other free pawn captures of hanging pieces (knights on c6/f3, even the enemy queen) that win material for a pawn.

243.label: Top: a king walks to a losing square—into a fork or off the passed pawn's path—turning a drawn/holdable endgame into a loss; medium broadens to any quiet endgame move (king or rook) that ignores a hanging piece or skips the only saving/drawing capture.

237.label: Top: a quiet king (or rook) move skips the one forced rook/queen trade—usually liquidating into a drawn or holdable PAWN endgame—so material is lost to a capture, very often with check (Rxc4+, Rxc2, Rxg7+); medium keeps the 'failed to make the critical capture/trade' core but blurs into middlegame tactics—walking into knight forks and discovered attacks, plus a few materially-safe moves that just miss a winning trade.

252.label: Top boards uniformly hang an undefended BISHOP in the opening — typically by ignoring/abandoning diagonal tension (the move's defender) when the correct play was a bishop trade/capture (Bxd2+, Bxe2, Bxg4), punished by a simple opponent bishop capture; medium blurs the piece (also knight, queen, rook left hanging by a deserting defender) and dilutes into tempo-loss, king-safety, and positional slips rather than pure free-piece drops.

249.label: Top: a won endgame is thrown away by an imprecise move—wrong check square, premature promotion, move-order slip, or hanging one's own piece—instead of the decisive forcing line; medium narrows specifically to mutual hanging-piece positions where the player fails to capture first and loses their own piece.

254.label: Top: queen sacrifices delivered with check (Qxg7+/Qg8+ type) that hang the queen for at most a pawn when the king just recaptures/escapes; medium broadens to rook and knight checks—plus a few non-checking forcing moves and skipped wins—where the same speculative attack fails to a calm king move or capture, leaving material lost.

259.label: Top: in winning opening positions, overlooks an undefended enemy BISHOP that a pawn could simply capture (dxc4, exf4, cxb4, fxg5), playing a routine developing move instead; medium broadens to other free hanging minor pieces (e.g. knight via Qxh4/hxg4) and non-pawn captures, but the core is the same missed free-piece grab.

261.label: Top: in a balanced/drawn endgame the player gives a rook check (e.g. Rg7+) that leaves the rook undefended for a free capture; medium blurs to any move that hangs material to a short 2-3 move tactical refutation, including non-rook/non-check moves like bxc3.

264.label: At the peak, the winning side plays a materially-safe but tempo-wasting move (often a wrong-square check or passive king/knight step) that lets a forced win or mate slip toward a draw/fortress; at medium activation it blurs into any slow tempo-losing move (knight retreats, pawn pushes) that merely concedes the advantage, diluted by several 0cp non-blunders flagged as 'tempo loss'.

268.label: Top boards are pure back-rank rook mate-in-one oversights (Rc1#/Rg1#/Ra1#) declined for a routine capture or king move; medium stays mate-in-one but blurs toward broader king-safety mates (e.g. diagonal Qf5#) and near-mate inaccuracies in already-winning positions.

258.label: Top: king steps directly onto an attacked diagonal/file, allowing a queen-winning or mating discovered check; medium broadens to line-opening pawn captures or removed-defender moves and to adjacent king-exposure tactics (forks-with-check, back-rank mates).

267.label: Top: a slow developing/castling move squanders a winning central pawn break (d4/d5/e5) that forks two minor pieces; medium: the same instinct skips a forcing pawn thrust (f4/b5/d6/f5/d5) that wins a single target or tempo rather than a clean two-piece fork.

269.label: Top: in a R+P endgame the player pushes a pawn or shuffles the king instead of the one critical capture/sacrifice (Rxa2+, Rxd2) that neutralizes the opponent's far-advanced passer, letting it promote; medium broadens to any rook/king move that abandons the blockade and still lets the pawn queen.

248.label: Top: a clearly won position where the player ignores a trivial one-move grab of a totally undefended rook (often a queen instead) — pure chess-blindness; medium: still a free rook being passed up, but via tempting checks, defender-removing pawn pushes, or 2-3 move refutations, and the move sometimes hangs the player's own piece rather than merely declining the capture.

241.label: Top boards are king moves that surrender control/blockade of an enemy pawn's promotion square (often allowing immediate queening with check) in a drawn endgame; medium broadens to other defending pieces — rook, queen, bishop — that fail to cover the queening square and let the pawn promote.

257.label: Top: a winning side trades off its dominant queenside piece via a greedy capture (Qxb1, Bxb3) that relieves all the pressure it had built; medium broadens to non-capturing queen repositioning (Qb5) that likewise hands back a won advantage, with the wider feature scattering into outright material-losing captures and king-safety hangs.

260.label: Top: a knight capture/move in a drawn or decided endgame that forces a transition into a LOST pure King+Pawn ending (the knight is swapped off, sometimes via an exchange sac); medium blurs to any simplifying trade or capture — and even weakening pawn pushes or a hung bishop — that surrenders the advantage without necessarily reaching a pure pawn ending.

265.label: Top boards play a quiet/preparatory move that neglects a tactical demand—often a missed ...Bxf2+ intermezzo or an ignored pin on f3—dropping a clean piece or the exchange to a forcing reply; medium broadens to moving the queen or another piece directly into an overlooked capture or fork.

262.label: Top: advancing one's own passed pawn (d6) is materially safe but throws away the win by skipping the tactic; medium blurs into loosening pawn breaks that challenge/create a passer and either hang material (c6→Qxb6) or concede a key square (h5→Kg5), with two piece-move outliers (Rc4, Qb3) lowering coherence.

272.label: Top: a pawn push/development ignores an enemy knight hanging to a pawn (often the d5 outpost); medium keeps the loose-knight theme but broadens the capturer to other pieces (e.g. Qxa4) with the knight wriggling out via a trade.

263.chip: Spoiled win with a check (often queen)
263.label: Top boards are queen checks that throw away a forced mate (or hang the queen) by chasing a tempting check instead of the cleanest win; medium blurs to rook/bishop/knight checks (and a few non-checks) that either hang material to a zwischenzug/recapture or just miss a faster mate/win — so it mixes hung-own with missed-win cases.

274.label: Top: in a won endgame, a king/pawn move ignores a free capture (often a hanging rook/queen) that would force mate, downgrading mate to 'merely winning'; medium: the same fire blurs to inefficient king/pawn moves that just waste tempo and lose conversion efficiency in already-won endgames.

266.label: Top boards are passive queen retreats (tempo loss) that abandon the only active counterplay/defense in single-good-move positions; medium broadens to other safe-looking moves (a wrong recapture allowing mate, a pawn push losing the passer) that likewise discard the sole holding/winning resource, conceding material or mate over the refutation.

273.label: Top: a quiet, greedy, or careless move that ignores the critical tactic/attack in a balanced or won position (e.g. Ne6 missing the queen-grab Nxh5, or Nxd4 ignoring the kingside assault); medium: this blurs into structural pawn moves (b6/f6/b4) that voluntarily weaken the position and hand the opponent a ~180–270cp advantage — a genuinely mixed bag spanning hanging-piece, king-safety, tempo, and positional themes.

276.label: TOP: in pure king-and-pawn endgames the king goes the wrong way / one tempo short of the enemy passed pawn (out of its 'square') and loses the promotion race, throwing away a won position; MEDIUM keeps the lost-race / wasted-tempo theme but blurs the piece and setting — rook endgames (rook decoupling from its passer, allowing deflection into a lost K+P ending), wrong checks/knight moves, and premature pawn pushes, plus a couple of off-theme king-safety/missed-capture blunders.

279.label: Top: a quiet developing/castling move ignores unresolved central tension and lets the opponent play the thematic e5 (or fxe5) break, which gains tempo/space and forks or wins material—best move was almost always to capture and resolve the tension first (dxe4/exf4/exd4/dxe5); medium broadens to other pawn breaks (f5, c4, g4) and tension-ignoring/defender-removing moves, with a few cases shading into pure tactical losses or a missed counter-break.

275.label: Top boards are knight sorties/grabs in an equal opening that hang the piece or strip a defender into a fork; medium broadens to natural bishop/queen developments that ignore an enabled tactic (pin, attack on a weak square) and lose material over the next moves.

281.label: Top: in a 100%-won endgame, plays a tempo-losing rook check (or pawn shuffle) instead of the clinical winning move — usually immediate queen promotion — squandering a forced mate or win; medium blurs to the same spurned-promotion check costing only minor tempo (mate-in-7 to mate-in-11).

282.label: At the peak the player blows a 100%-drawn endgame with a sharp material/holding error (king move hanging the rook, or failing to trade rooks into a theoretical draw); at medium it blurs into materially-safe but losing positional pawn pushes (g6+, h5) that collapse the drawn structure.

271.label: Top: a greedy material-grabbing capture (knight/bishop/pawn) in a winning position that abandons king or back-rank defense and is refuted by a decisive king attack or mate; medium broadens to quieter king-exposing moves (passive bishop retreat, king walk) punished by king attacks, perpetuals, or back-rank threats.

277.label: Top: a won K+piece endgame is thrown into an insufficient-material draw because the player captures/promotes on the passed pawn and loses the only mating piece (queen recaptured, knight underpromotion, bishop or rook taken back) → K(+minor) vs K; medium narrows to the rook-endgame case where grabbing the passer (Rxe5) drops the rook to a check/skewer, with two outliers (pawn-endgame opposition loss, minor king-placement slip) blurring the edges.

287.label: At the peak it's an unsound knight grab/sac near the enemy king — overwhelmingly Nxf7 (premature Fried-Liver) plus Nxf2, refuted by a plain Kxf7/Kxf2 that nets a piece for a pawn; at medium it blurs to other greedy opening captures and developing moves (Nxe4, Bc4, Nxc6) that simply hang a knight or bishop to a one-move recapture.

280.label: Top: a king move (or check-blocking piece move) walks the king onto an open file/rank and gets mated by forced checks; medium broadens to king moves that merely allow a drawing perpetual check or a knight fork winning material rather than delivering mate (plus some pure piece-hangs like Nd5/Bd4 blur the edges).

284.label: Top: a minor piece (almost always a knight, e.g. Nf6/Nc3) is left en prise to a direct e/d-pawn capture in the opening, either by moving it there or ignoring the threat; medium keeps the 'minor piece dropped to a capture' core but blurs to bishops, middlegame positions, greedy pawn-grabs, and tactical combinations (e.g. Rxd4) that net the material.

283.chip: Misplaced king hangs material (queen at medium)
283.label: TOP is uniformly a KING move to a bad square that abandons a defended piece/pawn or steps into a mating net (e.g. Kg7→Rxe6, Kf7→Rxc6, Ke8/Kf3/Ke2 walking into mate); MEDIUM blurs to QUEEN/major-piece sorties and greedy pawn-grabs (Qxb7, Qxb2, Qb5) that lose material or get the queen chased/trapped, plus a few king-into-check moves.

285.label: Top boards squander a winning/near-winning position with one decisive quiet move that gets sharply refuted — queen/piece sorties to passive or fork/mate-vulnerable squares (Qb5, Re1→Nf3+, Bb4→Nd5, king-exposing f6/Qb8/Qg5+); medium blurs into lower-severity positional squanders (knight off the e5 outpost, pawn moves ignoring a threat, a forkable Qe2, even a near-harmless king step), so the unifying thread is 'misplaced/abandoned piece throws away an advantage' but the material-vs-positional and hang-vs-missed split is genuinely mixed (hangs 50% / safe 50%).

294.chip: Hangs material on quiet move (often king)
294.label: Top: a 'safe' king retreat to a quiet square that hangs material (or allows mate) by skipping the saving/winning capture — typically an available queen capture; medium broadens the moving piece to queen, bishop and pawn pushes and includes slower endgame drift that likewise ignores the key capture/threat.

290.label: Top boards are queenside pawn pushes (a3/b4, also b3/b5/c6) attacking a knight or bishop that expect a passive retreat but backfire — the piece counterattacks/jumps or the move opens a fork/capture losing material (a couple instead miss a winning fork, e.g. Qa4/Qb4+); medium keeps the 'chase the enemy piece for a tempo' theme but broadens the move type (central pawn pushes like e5/e6/g4/h6/dxe4, even piece moves like Ke1/Re2/Nxe4) and the refutation type (discovered attacks, positional concessions, king-safety collapses) rather than a clean fork.

292.chip: Hangs to king-loosening move (often pawn push)
292.label: Top boards are sharp self-weakening moves around the king (f4/g4 pushes, reflexive checks like Ng3+/Nf4+, d6 opening lines) refuted by forcing attacks that win material; medium broadens to looser king-safety lapses, including a plainly hung pawn (Nxg4) and a king misplaced into a winning invasion.

295.label: Top: a greedy capture or king/queen move strips the king's own defense and is punished by a decisive forcing check (Qb5+/Qa4+/Qf7+ fork or back-rank mate); medium broadens to vacating any defender — retreating or repositioning a piece that simply leaves a knight/pawn/rook hanging without the king-attack element.

302.label: Top: a bishop sortie to an undefended rim square (Ba6/Bh6/Bh3, usually a misguided attempt to block a fianchetto or 'attack' b7/b2) hangs the piece for free in the opening; medium keeps the identical Ba6/Bh6 free-capture pattern.

270.label: Top: a direct queen-vs-queen standoff where the player ignores the free QxQ (often via a fleeing king move) and frequently hangs their own queen too; medium broadens to declining a hanging enemy queen capturable by a minor piece/pawn/rook for a smaller swing, sometimes grabbing lesser material instead.

300.label: Top boards show a piece sent to a passive or wrong square in an already-losing endgame (king to the h3 corner, the wrong rook to f4, a drifting bishop) that surrenders activity rather than centralizing; medium narrows to a structure-weakening pawn push (d4) that likewise concedes piece activity — note the SEE 'bishop/hangs 100%' signature contradicts the per-board analyses, which are positional, not material, hangs.

289.label: At the peak the player almost uniformly passes up a decisive forcing KNIGHT check/fork (Nf5+, Nf3+, Nxa2+, Nb3+, Nd6+, Nxf5+) in favor of a quiet/passive move, skipping a winning tactic; at medium the engine's saving resource blurs to non-knight forcing moves (rook checks like Rd7+, quiet positional shots g4/h4/Re1) and the error itself broadens from pure missed-win into greedy/positional blunders that actually hang material (Bxd4+ smothered mate, Kd7 dropping the bishop).

301.label: Top boards are uniform: the player ignores an opponent's passed pawn about to queen (usually abandoning or failing to move the sole blockading/defending rook), losing material to a capture-then-promote refutation; medium boards keep the 'hangs material by overlooking the urgent threat' core but broaden the threat from promotion to any tactical refutation — pins, back-rank mates, exchange sacs, and tempo-winning attacks on an undefended piece.

288.label: Top boards center on a bishop pushed forward in a drawn middlegame that simply drops (a capture-check sac on e6, or a Bd4/Rd4 'attacking' move that's snapped off) — broadening at the peak to a rook hang and even pure tempo-losing advances (premature d6+, passive Ke1); medium narrows to the prototypical bishop parked on d4 and taken for free by a knight.

297.chip: Hangs piece into knight's capture (often bishop)
297.label: Top boards quietly relocate a minor piece — most often a bishop developed/retreated, or a knight pulled off a good square — straight into an enemy knight's clean capture that wins material; medium broadens to unfavorable knight trades, knight forks, and quiet relocations that merely surrender the initiative or a winning advantage rather than hanging outright.

299.label: Top boards are king-exposing quiet moves (king steps or pawn pushes like Kh7/Kf5/b3/c5 that open a line or square near the own king) which invite a decisive check and forced mate; medium broadens to any self-weakening move (piece retreat, pawn push, tempo loss) that opens a line/vacates a square/removes a guard, losing material or a tactic rather than specifically the king.

293.label: Top: a natural recapture/developing move in an equal opening overlooks a tactic costing a full piece (often a knight — missing Qxe4+/Qxa5 or allowing Nd5); medium blurs to the same quiet opening moves (Nb5, Be7) leaking a pawn/material to an enemy knight tactic, with a couple of tops being purely positional/tempo losses.

303.label: Top: quiet flank-pawn pushes or bishop retreats (Ba5, c6, a6, b5/b6) that ignore a concrete tactic and trap/hang a piece — often a bishop; medium broadens to any slow non-forcing piece/pawn move that throws away the eval, mixing in tempo-loss/positional collapses and a couple of missed wins (Rxd6, Nxg5 mate).

306.label: Top: a winning side squanders a forced mate (or decisive blow) by playing a slow, non-forcing repositioning move—frequently a queen/king shuffle that loses tempo; medium blurs into merely missing faster material grabs and general positional/tempo imprecision in already-winning positions, plus a few non-errors and self-inflicted tactics.

305.label: Top boards are a grab-bag of quiet non-capturing moves that throw away a winning/equal position—missing forced wins (Rh8, dxe5) or playing strategically losing pawn/piece moves—while the lone medium board narrows specifically to hanging a piece by relocating it onto an attacked square (Nc4→Rxc5).

307.label: Top: a queen check left en prise and immediately captured (hangs the queen for nothing); medium broadens to other pieces hung (rook/bishop/knight, incl. via fork) and to forcing checks that squander a forced mate or winning advantage.

311.label: Top boards almost uniformly hang a ROOK to a BISHOP on a freshly-opened/long diagonal (exchange loss, mostly in the opening — by moving the rook onto it, vacating the blocker, or ignoring the bishop); medium keeps the open-diagonal-capture theme but blurs the victim to other pieces (knight, bishop) and the attacker beyond bishops (queen), plus a few non-diagonal slips (positional/king-safety).

309.label: Top boards make a move in a losing position that exposes the own king to a forcing check/discovered-check sequence ending in mate or a king-hunt (Bxf2+, Rxe8#, Rxd3#); medium boards keep the same check-driven king-exposure motif but the punishment nets material (Qxf5+ winning the rook, Rxh7+/Bxg6+) or merely concedes tempo (h4) rather than forced mate.

304.label: Top boards consistently neglect king safety—an uncastled/exposed king punished by a direct attack (Greek-Gift Bxh7+, opened diagonal/file, en-passant rip); medium blurs this into any defensive lapse, where a developing or pawn move vacates a piece/pawn guarding a key square and concedes a fork, check, or tempo-losing attack.

314.label: Top boards are forcing queen/rook checks that drive the enemy king to safety and drop or delay an otherwise forced mate (R1d7→Ra8+, Bf1#→Be4+); medium blurs into any unnecessary check that merely wastes a tempo or concedes small material/efficiency in still-winning middlegames and endgames, with many firings being 0cp 'best' checks rather than true blunders.

310.label: Top boards are kings stepping into a mating net (king-safety blunders where the king walks to a fatal square); medium broadens to any piece (rook/bishop/queen) hung to a tempo-gaining check or deflection, plus a few materially-safe moves that miss a forced win/mate.

312.label: Top boards consistently miss a forcing sacrificial blow (Rxf7/Rxg2 exchange sacs, Nxf2) by substituting a slow non-forcing move; medium broadens to any squandered win — free pawns, hanging pieces, knight forks, move-order finesses — plus slow positional drift and occasional outright hangs of own material.

308.label: Top: a premature/faulty forcing check—usually a knight fork (Nf6+/Ne7+/Nxf7+)—that the opponent refutes by capturing the checker (hanging the piece) or that squanders a forced mate; medium blurs to broader king-safety errors, including king moves that walk into checks/mate and defensive lapses, with only a minority still being checks.

298.label: Top: a queen/rook move forces a simplifying exchange that collapses into a concretely lost or drawn endgame (queen trade most common, rook trade close behind); medium keeps the throw-away-trade idea (dissolving a mating attack or a winning edge) but broadens to major/minor pieces simply hung to forcing tactics — removed defender, deflection, back-rank, intermezzo — plus a few missed tactical wins.

318.label: Top: a queen move (or queen-exposing move) drops the queen to a forcing check or knight-fork refutation; medium keeps the queen-losing tactics but broadens to losing a rook/exchange (and a few king-safety/mate motifs) via skewers, simple captures, and forks.

321.label: Top mixes coffeehouse Bxf2+ and Bxf7+ sacrifices that give a whole bishop for one pawn against an uncastled king; medium narrows to the purely unsound Bxf7+ ('Fried-Liver'-style) sac refuted by Kxf7.

319.label: Top boards are won/drawn pawn endgames where a slow king or pawn move squanders the position by skipping the urgent, often now-or-never, capture (e.g. Kf4 vs Kxf3, g3 vs Kxh7); medium broadens to rook/knight/bishop endgames and move-order/prophylaxis tempo errors that hand the opponent the tempo to equalize or win.

316.label: Top boards are knight moves shoved into a clean capture (Nd6/Nd3+/Ng6) while already losing; medium broadens to other pieces (Bg2 hanging the bishop) and king moves walking into mating nets — all worsening an already-lost position.

322.label: Top boards are all missed knight leaps (Nd4/Nd5/Nxe4) that fork an exposed enemy queen—usually on f3—and a second piece in the opening; medium blurs this to any piece or pawn hitting a misplaced queen on various squares (b6/c6/a5/g6/b4), with a couple of self-hanging moves mixed in.

323.label: Knight jumps to a 'fork' square that is actually defended, so it's captured for free; the very top peaks on Nc7+ royal forks refuted by Qxc7 (queen guards c7), while most top boards and the medium board are Nxf7 Fried-Liver sacrifices refuted by the simple Kxf7.

317.chip: Hangs pawn skipping central capture (often cxd5/dxe5)
317.label: TOP: in opening central pawn tension, plays a quiet developing/prep move (Bg2, Nc3, d3, a3) instead of the winning central capture cxd5/dxe5, hanging a pawn; MEDIUM keeps the 'skipped a needed capture in a tense opening' core but broadens the capture (en passant dxc6, queenside cxb4/axb5, recaptures Nxe4) and the lazy move (castling, rook lifts, pawn pushes), with more cases simply missing a forced win rather than outright hanging material.

313.label: Top boards: a rook capture/move in a losing endgame that hangs the rook itself (recaptured via promotion or lost to a skewer, sometimes also throwing away a forced mate); medium broadens to a passive rook move that instead drops an undefended minor piece to a tactic.

320.label: Top boards uniformly miss a free capture of the hanging enemy queen (overwhelmingly the e5-pawn taking on f6); medium boards retain the squandered-winning-position theme but blur to broader tactical oversights — allowing forks, hanging own pieces over 2-3 moves, or missing smaller positional wins.

327.label: At the peak it's near-identical ...Bxb4 pawn-grabs that abandon the f8-bishop's guard of g7, letting Bxg7 win the exchange down the long diagonal; medium broadens to other greedy bishop captures (e.g. Bxc5) that abandon a central pawn (e4), losing a pawn to a fork.

332.label: Top boards consistently miss a forced CHECKMATE—throwing the win away by grabbing material or an idle king/queen move that lets the loser draw by perpetual; medium boards keep the missed-forced-mate core but broaden to skipping forcing checks (Qd8+, Qe6+, Rd2+ zwischenzug) that win a rook or pawn rather than only mate.

333.label: Top: in a won endgame promotion race, the player passes up the immediate queening (very often the queen-with-check that wins on the spot), usually shuffling the king instead; medium broadens to looser promotion-timing errors — delaying one's own promotion by a tempo, allowing the opponent to queen with interposition, or trading/capturing into a lost pawn endgame.

326.label: Top: a winning side plays a quiet/prophylactic luft pawn move (g3, h3, g6, c6) and skips a forced mate or material-winning check/capture; medium blurs to any natural plan-based move (king walks, rook/bishop shuffles, premature pawn pushes) that throws away the win or, increasingly, allows a refuting zwischenzug or outright hangs material.

329.label: At the peak the feature fires on a quiet, non-forcing move (passive piece retreat, weakening pawn push, or king/queen misstep — best reply is always positional, never a material grab) that throws away a winning or clearly-better position by handing the opponent active counterplay/initiative; at medium the same advantage-squandering blurs to include outright material loss (Rc8 hanging to Qxf8+) and pure tempo loss (Rde1).

334.label: Top: tempo-losing pawn push or passive king move that forfeits king activity in a won/holdable king-and-pawn endgame (push wrong pawn instead of penetrating/racing); medium narrows to the king blockading enemy passers instead of advancing one's own decisive passed pawn.

335.label: Top boards are uniformly a missed Qh4+/Qh5+ check exploiting the open diagonal left by an absent/advanced f-pawn; medium boards keep that king weakness but broaden to wider tactics on it — Bxf7+ sacs, Qa4+ forks, queen traps, and Qh4+ with knight-fork follow-ups.

315.label: Top: ignored a free en-prise enemy minor — usually an intruding bishop that needed (re)capturing — by playing a quiet developing or pawn move, leaving it to escape; medium broadens to skipping other critical captures (knights, pawns, rook-takes-pawn, defensive resources) and mixes in a few greedy captures that instead hang the player's own material.

325.label: Top: a routine developing/castling move ignores an undefended enemy bishop (f5/d6/c5) capturable for a clean piece; medium: the same skipped-capture pattern broadens to free knights and pawns, plus occasional tactical wins, and a few cases that tip into hanging one's own material to short forks/Greek-gift shots.

331.label: Top: a rook move hangs material to a clean capture/back-rank or open-file tactic in an already-difficult middlegame; medium broadens to other pieces — e.g., a knight self-blocking the king and allowing mate.

338.label: Top boards uniformly miss a one-move capture of a completely hanging enemy QUEEN while already winning; medium broadens to grabbing any free hanging piece (knight/bishop/pawn-fork) or choosing the more decisive winning capture.

343.label: Top: in pure pawn endgames the (already losing) king marches the wrong way—passive/centralizing instead of counterattacking enemy pawns—forfeiting the critical tempo race; medium broadens to other endgame types (rook, king-safety/mate-walks) and to tempo-wasting non-king moves (a6, Bd4), where the same one-tempo lag decides the race.

341.label: Top: in a clearly winning position the player hangs a MAJOR piece (usually the queen or a rook), almost always by moving its sole defender or parking it en prise, flipping a win into a loss; Medium: blurs to hanging any piece (incl. minors/pawns over 2-3 moves and walking into forks) AND to merely squandering the win via a safe but tempo-losing/suboptimal move that misses the stronger continuation.

342.label: Top is constant: a piece/pawn lost in the open-game opening, usually a greedy central capture immediately recaptured (Nxd4, Nxe5, Bxd4, exd4) or a developing/attacking move that ignores a one-move shot (Bxg7, Bxf7+, Qxc3+, pawn fork); medium blurs into materially-safe moves that squander the advantage by missing the forcing win or correct move order (Bb5+ winning the queen, Bg3+, Re8+ first) alongside a few more middlegame hangs.

339.label: Top: the queen quits the king's defense—usually a greedy a-file/queenside pawn-grab—and is lost or allows mate; medium broadens to any misplaced piece (wrong recapture, allowing a fork, leaving a dominant square) that hangs material or squanders the advantage.

349.label: Top boards are greedy material-grabs (usually capturing a piece/queen) that overlook an immediate mate-in-1; medium broadens to missing longer forced mates (M2–M8) and includes non-capturing repositioning moves that throw away the win.

346.label: Top boards hang a knight outright by jumping it to an undefended aggressive square (Nf5/Nh5 simply captured by bishop/queen) from a winning position; medium blurs this into knight sorties that instead lose tempo, get chased, or walk into a fork/mate—with a couple of non-knight or missed-win cases muddying it.

345.label: Top boards are uniformly missed knight forks hitting BOTH rooks to win the exchange in a winning position; medium keeps the knight-wins-the-exchange motif but blurs to single-rook/other knight shots (Nxf6, Nh7) and occasional cases where the played move instead hands the opponent the exchange.

344.label: Top: an aggressive opening capture/check (overwhelmingly Bxf7+ or a wrong-order recapture) hangs a minor piece to the opponent's in-between move (zwischenzug like exf6/Bxd8); medium keeps the 'forcing move that loses material' core but blurs to assorted forcing-move blunders—checks that hang the piece, failed fork attempts, self-pins, and even missed captures that squander a win.

340.label: At the peak the move relocates an active piece (most often a knight) onto a square where it hangs to a tactical/checking refutation in a worse position; at medium it broadens into king-walks into checks and multi-move pawn losses, with a couple of missed-win/missed-mate cases mixed in.

324.label: Top: a quiet, non-forcing middlegame move (repositioning/pawn push) overlooks a tactic, usually leaving a minor piece hanging—with the two peak boards instead missing a winning knight/bishop shot (Bg4/Ng4); medium broadens to hanging pawns, knights and the exchange, plus endgame king-march and deflection/king-safety tactics.

354.label: Top boards are defensive king/pawn moves in a losing endgame that ignore an immediate mating net and walk into forced checkmate (king_safety/back_rank); medium broadens the same 'unaddressed threat' pattern to a move that concedes a decisive material-winning tactic rather than mate.

336.label: Top: safe-looking king/knight moves in drawn endgames that hang a rook/major piece to an invasion over the 2-3 move refutation; medium blurs into king-safety collapses allowing mate and near-trivial tempo/opposition slips.

352.label: Top: rook captures a (passed) pawn WITH CHECK, sacrificing the last defender in a lost endgame; medium keeps the rook-for-pawn liquidation but drops the check and even broadens to a losing pawn-endgame race.

353.label: Top boards consistently move a piece off its defensive post (queen/rook/knight) so the now-loose unit is grabbed by a forcing open-file capture, most often Rxe1+/Rxd8+ on the e/back rank; medium boards keep the 'abandons defense, loses material to a forcing line' core but blur into back-rank mates (Qxg2+), trapped pieces (Nb2), and other ignored tactical threats.

356.label: Top boards auto-promote a pawn to queen in a won endgame straight into immediate checkmate against the player's own king (back-rank Rh8# or enemy counter-promotion b1=Q#), ignoring the required defensive/king move; medium blurs to promotions that merely allow a perpetual-check draw (Qxg5+) or otherwise squander the cleanest forced win rather than getting mated outright.

357.label: Top boards leave the queen undefended/abandoned to a direct attack in an already-losing position; medium broadens to a pawn push (f4) that hangs a minor piece by overlooking the counter-tactic.

351.label: Top: in a dead-drawn endgame the king marches the wrong way into a mating net (Kg6/Ka3, missing the saving Kxf8/centralization); medium broadens to any endgame move that throws the result—still wrong-way king moves (Kh6) but now also pawn pushes like g4 that open a decisive breakthrough.

359.label: Top: while winning, grabs material with an immediate rook/queen capture instead of the forcing intermediate check or zwischenzug that forces mate; medium broadens to any tempo-wasting move (quiet queen/pawn pushes, or a capture that hangs the queen) that squanders a forced mate.

348.label: Top: a passive move in a winning middlegame lets the enemy rook reach the 7th rank and snatch queenside pawns (b7/a7), collapsing the advantage; medium broadens to other rook penetrations (kingside Rh8, Re7+) and small-swing inaccuracies, with a couple of plain piece/pawn hangs blurring the pattern.

358.label: Top: a rook grabs an advanced passed pawn with check and is recaptured by the king (Rxg7+/Rxa7+/Rxc7+) in king-and-pawn endings; medium keeps the 'capture the dangerous passer and get it taken' idea but broadens the piece/check (queen Qxa7+, bishop Bxb3, non-check Rxa6/Rxd7), so the constant is rook-takes-passer-with-check and what blurs is the capturing piece and the check.

347.label: Top is a quiet non-capturing move that surrenders a winning/holdable position via two co-existing mechanisms — leaving a piece loose to be won over 1-3 moves (Nf6→Nxh4, Rde1→Rxh6, Nxd6 trapped, Nf3→Qxb2, d5→exd5) OR exposing/weakening the own king & structure (h3, Qh5, f6, Kg7); medium keeps the same boards but blurs further into pure positional concessions like abandoning a blockading bishop (Bc3) and letting an advantage slip (gxh4), so the underlying error type (material-hang vs king-safety vs positional) is genuinely mixed despite the SEE 'hangs 100%' signal.

361.label: Top: the player's own queen move walks into a queen-for-queen capture (often a greedy recapture or 'natural' check answered with check); medium broadens to any move—rook/bishop/knight/pawn—that leaves the queen hanging or opens the line for the enemy queen to win it or force a losing trade.

355.label: Top: a king move in an already-lost king-and-pawn endgame that fails the pawn race / can't catch the passer (often a 0–2cp 'non-blunder' where the loss is baked in); medium blurs to broader losing-position moves of any piece (king, rook, queen, pawn) whose collapse lets a passer queen, allows mate, or drops material to a fork.

365.label: Top: in winning endgames, declining to grab a completely undefended bishop (a free full piece, often via king or pawn capture); medium keeps the free-capture theme but broadens to other hanging pieces (knights, queens) plus a few marginal/positional borderline cases.

350.label: Top boards are quiet, non-forcing pawn/piece moves (h3, c3, a4, Ne5, b6) that throw away a clearly winning position by skipping the one precise forcing win/break; medium broadens to moves that more directly hang material or allow a concrete tactic (free capture, fork, king attack) from a roughly equal/unclear position.

363.label: Top: a king move (or ignored mate threat) walks into a forcing attack / outright checkmate; medium: the same king march merely loses material in an already-lost position.

372.label: Top: passed up the crushing Nxf7 knight sacrifice (Fried Liver) against an uncastled king, choosing a safe/prophylactic move instead; medium broadens to missing any winning knight tactic — sacs (Nxh2), forks (Nxc2), and captures (Nxg3) — across opening and middlegame.

371.label: Top boards consistently play a slow pawn/queen move that squanders the winning Qh5+ check punishing an opened e8–h5 king diagonal (after ...f5); medium broadens to other slow opening pawn moves that concede the analogous kingside-diagonal attack rather than the exact Qh5+ shot.

360.label: Top: an aimless rook/queen move—frequently a hollow check—skips the clean winning/saving capture, usually a queen or rook trade; medium keeps the 'avoided the one correct capture' core but broadens the played move to king/pawn passivity and occasionally hangs material or walks into mate.

367.label: Top boards are forced-mate misplays around the king (missing Qe8# / walking the king into Qh8#); medium broadens to a king move that loses the position without an immediate mate, and directions split (one missed win vs. two own-side collapses).

362.label: Top: a passive rook move squanders a winning passed-pawn endgame (lost tempo/missed the decisive capture or push); medium blurs to knight/bishop/king moves in the same won pawn races that outright hang material.

373.chip: Hangs material via slow move (tempo-loss→deserts defender)
373.label: Top: a tempo-losing repositioning move (king/rook/queen relocation) in a critical winning or pawn-race/king-attack position that lets the opponent's plan (passed-pawn push, skewer, or mating attack) win material; medium broadens to quiet moves that abandon a piece's defensive duty, directly hanging a piece or pawn.

370.chip: Hangs bishop via king retreat (any piece)
370.label: Top: in a winning position a king-safety retreat (off f7, or to g1) hangs the g4-bishop while missing the crushing ...Qxg5; medium broadens to other quiet/safety moves that throw away the win by hanging various pieces (knight forks, hung rooks, trapped bishop) or skipping the Qxg5 capture.

368.label: Top: a queen move vacates the king's key defensive square, allowing forced mate or a decisive king attack; medium keeps the queen-moves-king-exposed theme but blurs into greedy trades, plain hanging pieces, and even a few missed wins/false positives.

379.label: TOP: a minor piece (usually the fianchetto/dark-squared bishop) snatches a defended central pawn in the opening and is recaptured for free, losing a piece for a pawn; MEDIUM keeps the greedy opening pawn-grab but broadens to knight captures and indirect refutations — removing a defender, opening a diagonal, or a discovered attack that costs material 2-3 moves later.

376.label: Top: in won K+P endgames a premature pawn break/advance liquidates into a draw instead of centralizing/penetrating with the king; medium broadens to any committal or misplaced move (pawn push, king to the wrong square, piece relocation) that squanders a winning/better position by inviting blockade, liquidation, or counterplay.

374.label: Top: in king-and-pawn endgames the king greedily wanders off to snatch a pawn and falls out of the enemy passed pawn's square (or abandons a defensive square), losing the pawn race/draw; medium broadens to slower passive king-tempo moves and premature pawn pushes that misplace the king across mixed endgames, plus a few near-zero non-blunders.

378.label: Top boards are own queen promotions that backfire (queen captured by knight/bishop or walks into back-rank/self-mate); medium blurs to king/rook moves that instead let the opponent's passed pawn promote, frequently with check.

377.label: Top: bishop captures (often with check) that trade off an active attacking piece and invite a simplifying queen swap, squandering a winning edge or even a forced mate; medium broadens to knight/rook/pawn captures that release tension or greedily grab material and outright hang.

383.label: Top boards are all forward pawn thrusts (e5/d5/f3) that overextend and squander a winning/equal edge by getting refuted with an immediate capture or line-opening; medium narrows to the d5 central break that blows open the center against an uncastled king and costs material.

364.label: At the peak it's purposeless checks/king moves that waste a tempo and squander a roughly-equal-or-better position (Rc5+, Qd6+, Qf8); at medium it blurs into outright king-safety disasters—walking the king into mating nets/forks (Kf5, Kh1, O-O-O) and assorted hung pieces.

375.label: Top boards are near-uniform: an undefended enemy queen (rarely a rook) sits en prise and the player moves the very piece attacking it—or plays an unrelated king/pawn move—instead of the free capture; medium boards blur away from 'free queen' to ~400cp tactical blunders in roughly level positions, walking into a queen fork or exposing the king rather than choosing the best material-winning move.

380.label: Top: greedy queen captures that strip the sole back-rank defender and allow an immediate forced back-rank/file checkmate; medium: broader greedy material grabs (plus a few loosening pawn moves) punished by forks, pins, wrong-piece recaptures, or slower mating attacks.

391.label: Top boards uniformly skip a forcing check/sacrifice (deflection or clearance) that wins the opponent's QUEEN outright; medium boards keep the 'missed forcing shot' theme but broaden the prize to rooks, the exchange, or a forced mate, plus wrong move-order between two winning tactics.

382.label: At the peak a constructive-looking quiet move (or an only-move position) ignores a forcing attack on the player's own king or sole defense, getting mated or losing a piece/exchange to checks and forks; at medium strength it blurs into quieter deflections, pins, and tempo-losses that merely drop a pawn or surrender the initiative.

389.label: Top is pure pawn-endgame king moves that lose the opposition/tempo (turning won positions to draws or draws to losses); medium keeps the wrong-square king move but blurs into king-safety/mating-net walks and other endgames (rook endings, plus a couple non-king tempo/back-rank slips).

388.label: Top: a natural developing/castling/quiet move in the opening ignores an existing piece tension or attack on a minor piece (often the c4/e6 bishop standoff) and hangs it outright for a one-move capture; medium blurs this to pawns, fork/pin motifs and multi-move refutations, and increasingly to squandered winning positions where the quiet move misses a free capture rather than strictly hanging material.

386.label: Top: queen left undefended on an open file/diagonal (esp. d1) is won by a deflection/removal-of-guard sacrifice like Bxh2+...Rxd1; medium keeps the walk-into-a-tactic theme but broadens the spoils to queen-for-rook checks, forks, and hung minor pieces/pawns.

393.label: Top boards miss a FORCED MATE (often mate-in-1) by grabbing material / playing a quiet non-forcing move while completely winning; medium boards keep the same 'winning side plays a slow move' core but blur the goal — broadening from mate to any forcing win (winning a piece with check, gaining tempo, or a faster mate).

392.label: Top: in the opening Black's queen sits on d5 but retreats (Qd8/Qa5/Qd7) instead of grabbing the undefended d4 pawn with Qxd4 (or the equivalent Bxf3 win), conceding the center to a tempo-gaining d5 push; medium blurs into other missed central-pawn captures/tactics (Nxe4, Nxd4, Qh5+) and even passively letting the opponent win or push the central pawn.

385.label: Top boards consistently trade or hang a piece (rook/knight/queen) to capture a dangerous passed pawn in an endgame and lose material to the recapture; medium broadens to other mistimed endgame decisions—premature pawn pushes, king misplacement, or moving a piece into a fork—that squander a winning or holdable ending.

399.label: Top: unsound bishop sacrifice grabbing the h3/h6 pawn to rip open the enemy king's cover (refuted by simply taking, then Nh2); medium broadens to any unsound minor-piece sac or grab that hangs the piece — knight sacs on d5/b5, trapped/greedy bishops, and pawn pushes that drop a hanging minor.

397.label: Top: defender in a passed-pawn endgame loses the promotion race by trading off or mis-placing the only piece guarding the queening square (Rxc5, Bxd6, Rxf8, walking into Nc2+); medium narrows to losing the SAME race by burning a tempo or playing passively instead of a check/intermezzo (Bd6 vs Bc5+, d3 vs Rxe3+, Rh8 vs Rxc4).

390.label: At the peak the player hangs a full piece via a miscalculated active capture — an illusory fork refuted by simple recapture (Nxe5/Nxd3); medium boards broaden to passive king/pawn moves (Kh8, e4) that decline the winning capture and let the opponent favorably exchange or win material, with outlier top boards drifting into king-safety/tempo errors.

398.label: Top: a bishop (occasionally the queen) greedily captures a seemingly 'free' but defended pawn (b7/g7/c2/c7) in the opening and is lost for a pawn after the obvious recapture; medium blurs into other overambitious captures and pawn pushes that squander the advantage (positional, endgame, missed-tactic), so the clean 'hangs-bishop-on-pawn-grab' core no longer holds tightly.

400.label: At the peak the feature fires on clean minor-piece hangs in the opening—most often a knight moved to or capturing onto an undefended square (Nxe4, Nxd4, Nxd5, Ne2) and giving the piece away for free; at medium it blurs to other opening material losses, including a knight that hangs by blocking its own defender (Ne2) and a greedy pawn-grab (Nxb3) that loses a tempo/advantage rather than the piece outright.

396.label: Top: a passive/quiet move declines a forcing winning queen check (frequently capturing); medium broadens to any missed winning tactic—non-queen captures, non-checking grabs, rook checks—and bleeds into outright hanging own material.

401.label: Top: pure king-and-pawn endgames where advancing a pawn immediately hangs it to a capture, flipping a draw into a loss (or worsening a lost position); medium blurs into passed-pawn and bishop endgames where a premature/wrong-pawn push concedes material or a win — though several flagged boards are actually the best move, adding noise.

395.label: Top boards uniformly pass up a clean capture of the opponent's hanging/attacked queen (Bxd8, Bxd1, Nxd2) for a quiet developing/castling move; medium boards keep the same theme but blur to taking the lesser piece in a fork (Nxh8 not Nxd8) or grabbing a pawn/bishop instead of the available queen.

394.label: Top: a bishop trades off a centralized knight and the opponent's queen recaptures to a dominating central square, turning an even trade into a lost/blown winning advantage; medium broadens to other premature or greedy captures that ignore a stronger move — wrong move-order/zwischenzug, fork, back-rank, or passed-pawn race.

384.label: Constant across top & medium: a winning position where the h8-rook can grab White's queen on h5 (Rxh5) but a quiet pawn move (g6) lets Qxh8 win the rook; top broadens to queen on h4/h7 and pawn-captures (gxh4/gxh5) where the ignored free queen sometimes just escapes (pure missed win), making the direction mixed between hanging the rook and merely missing the queen.

387.label: Top boards are tempting captures/trades that liquidate the player's own key defensive piece (often simplifying straight into a lost endgame); medium boards broaden to quiet repositioning that misplaces a piece, losing tempo or walking into a fork.

402.label: At the peak a piece/pawn is hung to an immediate, forcing material-winning reply that's usually a check (Rxf6+, Bxd4+, Qg5+, or d5 hitting the just-moved Rc4); at medium the trigger blurs to quieter or multi-move refutations and tempo/positional collapses (exd5 simplification, Rxd3 winning the queen, Kc6 losing the pawn endgame) where material/advantage is conceded more slowly and without a check.

404.label: Top boards uniformly fail to play Nxd4 to resolve the Nd4–Nf3 (or Nd5) central tension and get punished by ...Nxe2+/...Nxf3+ forks-with-check or a dominant enemy knight; medium boards broaden to skipping any key centralized minor-piece capture/trade (Nxe5, Bxe4, Bxd5, exf4), allowing assorted knight forks, discovered checks, or lost material — and the direction blurs between hanging material and merely squandering a win.

407.label: Top boards make a king-exposing move (king-walk or abandoning the king's cover) that loses to a forced mating/checking attack in a winning-or-equal position; medium broadens to hanging a piece/queen to a capturing attack rather than mate.

408.chip: Hangs piece by ignoring center (often bishop)
408.label: Top: a just-developed minor piece (usually the bishop on c5/c4, sometimes a knight) sits on a square attacked by a pawn and is captured for free next move (dxc5/dxc4/dxc6) because central tension was neglected; medium broadens this to ignoring the central pawn tension more generally, conceding material or a winning attack over several moves rather than to a single immediate pawn grab.

413.label: Top boards uniformly hang a minor piece—almost always a bishop—by grabbing the 'annoying intruder' immediately instead of inserting the needed intermediate trade/check (zwischenzug) first; medium keeps the same wrong-order capture impulse but blurs the consequence to any material, king-exposing line-openings, or a skipped larger tactic.

410.label: At the peak it's a clean single-tempo error—usually a king move or wrong move-order in a winning/drawn endgame that lets the opponent's passed pawn queen at once (often with check or unstoppably); at medium it blurs to greedy captures and abandoned blockades where the passer promotes or forces a lost endgame a few moves later.

412.label: Top: a quiet/developing move ignores an immediate diagonal mating attack on the king (almost always a Qxh2#/Qxh7#/Qxg2#-type mate-in-one from a queen+bishop battery); medium broadens to quiet/natural moves that overlook any forcing threat winning material — a hung pawn or piece, the exchange via an opened long diagonal, a trapped queen, or a king attack netting material.

409.label: Top: a piece relocation to a seemingly active square (knight to outpost, king-walk, queen sortie) abandons defense of a key central pawn or the king and is refuted by immediate capture/attack; medium narrows to clear cases where a queen or rook vacates a square and leaves an adjacent pawn or piece hanging for free.

406.label: At the peak the move puts/leaves the king exposed to a single decisive check (Greek-gift Bxh7+, Qe4+/Qxb2+, Rf6+) that wins material or forces mate; at medium it blurs to the king walking into knight forks (Nd4+) plus a few non-king moves that hang material to a forcing sequence (tempo-attacked queen, self-blocked file, wrong-knight capture).

411.label: Top: a quiet developing/repositioning move (Bd2, castling, Be3) in a winning opening passes up a forcing pawn capture that wins a hanging knight (repeatedly exf6), letting the piece retreat to safety; medium keeps the 'declined a material-winning capture' core but broadens the target to bishops/pawns/exchange and blurs into cases where the chosen move actively hangs own material.

421.label: Top: in an already-lost position, ignores an own rook under direct attack (often by a bishop) — playing a king/rook move that leaves it to be captured for free instead of the forced recapture; medium broadens to hanging other pieces (knight, queen) and to tempo-losing king/bishop shuffles that merely accelerate a hopeless endgame rather than dropping a piece outright.

403.label: Top boards miss the unique winning queen/promotion check that would trap the enemy king (which instead sidesteps to safety, squandering mate/advantage); medium broadens from wrong-check king-escapes to any imprecise, tempo-wasting move that lets the opponent's king or position consolidate.

420.label: Top: a quiet bishop/king developing move ignores an enemy bishop that has invaded the own camp (b7/g7/b2), hanging a rook or the exchange; medium broadens to a general failure to recapture or grab an undefended bishop, hanging just the minor piece.

424.label: Top: in a won rook/pawn endgame the player plays an aimless rook move/check instead of the immediate king capture Kxh2 that grabs an undefended rook (king ideally placed to recapture the promoting g-pawn); medium blurs to near-equal rook checks (Ra2+) that merely delay the same winning Kxh2, and the captured target broadens from rook toward any hung piece (e.g., Kxe4 bishop).

414.label: Top boards are bishop captures/recaptures that squander a winning edge or rip open the player's own king after the reply; medium boards broaden to any capture (knight, pawn) that simply hangs a piece to the recapture.

415.label: Top: a materially-safe king/minor-piece move retreats from an active post or key square, surrendering the initiative and free tempi (positional/tempo loss); medium: the same square-abandonment broadens to more often enable a concrete tactic (fork, pin, or hanging pawn) that actually loses material.

417.label: At the peak the player relocates/weakens a piece guarding the KING (Rc5, g6, Qf6, Nb8), abandoning a defensive duty and walking into a forced mating attack; at medium the same 'active relocation' instinct (knight to an outpost, bishop reposition) instead just drops a defended pawn or the exchange — so the constant is 'moved a defender for an ambitious active square,' and what blurs is whether the abandoned charge was the king (mate) or ordinary material.

426.label: Top: a king retreats/misroutes in a passed-pawn endgame and lets the enemy pawn promote, often flipping a slow loss into forced mate (~9400cp); medium broadens to any wrong king move in a king-and-pawn (or minor-piece) endgame that surrenders tempo/opposition or the blockade for far smaller cost (60–250cp), with a couple of near-equal non-blunders mixed in.

428.label: Top boards are uniformly a missed mate-in-one, almost always a queen capture/check next to the king; medium broadens to missed longer forced mates (M2-M5, also bishop mates) and missed winning continuations, frequently by choosing an inferior check or wrong piece/square that squanders the forced win.

423.label: Top: pawn-endgame positions where a passive king move or wrong pawn push forfeits the one decisive lever (breakthrough/capture like e5, g6, cxb5, axb6), either missing the win/draw or allowing enemy passers to break through; medium keeps the skipped pawn-break theme (f5/b4/b5) but widens to rook/other endgames and tempo-losing king moves, with a couple of king-safety blunders blurring the pattern.

427.label: Top: forcing 'hope/desperation checks' that hand over a queen, rook, or bishop for nothing (usually in an already-lost position) with no follow-up attack; medium keeps the give-away-material theme but blurs the trigger to pawn-push or wrong-move-order checks and even quiet non-checking moves that hang a piece or ignore a mate/threat.
